tylosaurus-rex:table:1.title: 2026 in reptile paleontology (table of new taxa)

tylosaurus-rex:enwiki:6.title: Tylosaurus (Later discoveries and other species, part 2)

facts.statement: Tylosaurus rex is a mosasaur species belonging to the subfamily Tylosaurinae.
facts.quote: A mosasaur belonging to the subfamily Tylosaurinae; a species of Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus rex lived during the Late Cretaceous Campanian age.
facts.quote: Age: Late Cretaceous (Campanian)

facts.statement: The type locality of Tylosaurus rex is the Wolfe City Formation in Texas, United States.
facts.quote:
Type locality: Wolfe City Formation
Country: United States
Region: Texas

facts.statement: Tylosaurus rex is estimated to have reached over 13 m in length and weighed nearly 8.4 t, making it the largest species of the genus.
facts.quote: the largest of which, T. rex, estimated to have reached over 13 m long and weighed nearly 8.4 t.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus was established by Marsh in 1872.
facts.quote: authority: Marsh, 1872

facts.statement: Tylosaurus lived from about 92 to 66 million years ago, spanning the Turonian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous.
facts.quote: lived about 92 to 66 million years ago during the Turonian to Maastrichtian stages of the Late Cretaceous

facts.statement: Researchers suggest that Tylosaurus had an endothermic metabolism, which is unusual for squamates.
facts.quote: It had an endothermic metabolism, which is unlike nearly all modern squamates.

facts.statement: In 1885 Louis Dollo described the genus and species Hainosaurus bernardi based on an almost complete but poorly preserved skeleton from a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium (catalogue IRSNB R23).
facts.quote: In 1885, Louis Dollo described the genus and species Hainosaurus bernardi from an almost complete but poorly preserved skeleton discovered in a phosphate quarry in the Ciply Basin of Mesvin, Belgium, since numbered as IRSNB R23.

facts.statement: The genus name Hainosaurus means "lizard from the Haine" referring to the nearby river.
facts.quote: The genus name Hainosaurus means "lizard from the Haine", in reference to the eponymous river located nearby the Ciply Basin.

facts.statement: The specific epithet bernardi honors Leopold Bernard, who made the excavation of the specimen possible.
facts.quote: The specific epithet bernardi is named in honor of Leopold Bernard, who made the excavation and exhumation of the specimen possible.

facts.statement: In 1988 Elizabeth Nicholls described a second species historically assigned to Hainosaurus, based on the partial skeleton MT 2 from Manitoba, Canada, naming it after the Pembina Member of the Pierre Shale.
facts.quote: In 1988, a second species historically pertained to Hainosaurus was described by Elizabeth Nicholls based on a partial skeleton catalogued as MT 2 and having been discovered in Manitoba, Canada. The specific epithet refers to the type locality of the taxon, namely the Pembina Member of the Pierre Shale.

facts.statement: Johan Lindgren first discussed the attribution of H. pembinensis to Hainosaurus in 2005, and in a 2010 revision Bullard and Caldwell transferred it to Tylosaurus as T. pembinensis.
facts.quote: The attribution of H. pembinensis to Hainosaurus is first discussed by Johan Lindgren in 2005, but it was in a revision published in 2010 that the species was moved to Tylosaurus by Timon Bullard and Michael Caldwell, being then renamed as T. pembinensis.

facts.statement: In 2016 Paulina Jimenez‑Huidobro and Michael Caldwell redescribed H. bernardi and transferred it to Tylosaurus as T. bernardi.
facts.quote: This redescription was finally carried out by Paulina Jimenez-Huidobro and Caldwell in 2016, in which they transferred the species to Tylosaurus, being then renamed as T. bernardi.

facts.statement: Some authors continue to argue for maintaining Hainosaurus as a distinct genus, citing dental traits not addressed in the 2016 revision.
facts.quote: some authors nevertheless suggest continuing to maintain the genus Hainosaurus as distinct, justified in particular on the basis of dental traits not detailed in the 2016 revision.

facts.statement: In 2008 Caldwell and colleagues reported Taniwhasaurus in northern Japan, reaffirming dental similarities with the Ivö Klack species and reviving the hypothesis of a possible reassignment, though they left it for future study.
facts.quote: In 2008, Caldwell and colleagues reported the presence of Taniwhasaurus in northern Japan and reaffirmed the dental similarities with T. ivoensis. This discovery revived the hypothesis of a possible reassignment of the species to Taniwhasaurus, but the authors see this as a subject for another study.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus rex was formally described in 2026 based on numerous mostly complete fossils from Texas and Kansas that had previously been assigned to T. proriger.
facts.quote: In 2026, Zietlow, Polcyn, and Tykoski described the species T. rex based on numerous more or less complete fossil specimens discovered in the fossil record of Texas and Kansas, which had previously been assigned to T. proriger.

facts.statement: The holotype of Tylosaurus rex is a partial skeleton preserving a complete skull (catalogue PMNS 8029) discovered in 1979 in Lake Ray Hubbard, Texas.
facts.quote: The holotype consists of a partial skeleton preserving, among other remains, a complete skull catalogued as PMNS 8029, discovered in 1979 in Lake Ray Hubbard, a reservoir located east of Dallas.

facts.statement: The exact stratigraphic position of the T. rex holotype is uncertain, but its locality indicates it came from the Wolfe City Formation.
facts.quote: Its exact stratigraphic position is uncertain, but its locality indicates that it originated from the Wolfe City Formation.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus was a derived mosasaur with a fully aquatic lifestyle, possessing a streamlined body, an elongated tail with a two‑lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.
facts.quote: It had a streamlined body, an elongated tail ending with a downturn supporting a two-lobed fin, and two pairs of flippers.

facts.statement: Derived mosasaurs like Tylosaurus convergently evolved body shapes similar to ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and early whales.
facts.quote: they were more similar in build to other large marine vertebrates such as ichthyosaurs, marine crocodylomorphs, and archaeocete whales through convergent evolution.

facts.statement: Across the species, Tylosaurus rex individuals range in length from about 7.7 m to 13.2 m.
facts.quote: with the species as a whole ranging between 7.7-13.2 m

facts.statement: Specimens previously assigned to T. proriger that are now recognized as T. rex have caused the size range for T. proriger to be revised downward to 3.9–9.5 m.
facts.quote: the size estimates of T. proriger have since been revised to lower ranges of between 3.9-9.5 m

facts.statement: By the early Campanian, Tylosaurus rex individuals attained lengths of about 13–14 m.
facts.quote: attained lengths of 13-14 m

facts.statement: Everhart suggested that, because mosasaurs grew continuously, some exceptionally old Tylosaurus could have reached up to 20 m, but no fossil evidence supports such extreme size.
facts.quote: it would have been possible for some extremely old Tylosaurus individuals to reach 20 m in absolute maximum length. However, he stressed the lack of fossil evidence suggesting such sizes

facts.statement: The holotype of T. bernardi has recent maximum length estimates of 12.2 m (Lindgren 2005) and 11.6 m (Zietlow et al. 2026), though older estimates placed it at 15–17 m.
facts.quote: holotype of T. bernardi are 12.2 m by Lindgren (2005) and 11.6 m by Zietlow et al. (2026); historically the species was erroneously estimated at even larger sizes of 15-17 m

facts.statement: T. gaudryi has been estimated at about 7.1 m in length, T. kansasensis between 2.9 and 7 m, and T. iembeensis around 5.5 m.
facts.quote: T. gaudryi, T. kansasensis and T. iembeensis have been estimated around 7.1 m, 2.9-7 m and 5.5 m respectively

facts.statement: A reconstruction of T. saskatchewanensis suggests a total length exceeding 9.75 m.
facts.quote: estimated a total length of over 9.75 m

facts.statement: The mounted T. pembinensis skeleton “Bruce” measures 13.05 m and held the 2014 Guinness World Record for the largest mosasaur on display, although later work showed its vertebral count had been exaggerated.
facts.quote: measures at 13.05 m long and was awarded a Guinness World Records for "Largest mosasaur on display" in 2014. However, the skeleton was assembled for display prior to Bullard and Caldwell (2010)'s reassessment that found the species' number of vertebrae to be exaggerated

facts.statement: Specimens referred to T. "borealis" are estimated to be between 6.5 and 8 m long.
facts.quote: T. "borealis" is estimated at 6.5-8 m in total length

facts.statement: The largest known Tylosaurus skull, belonging to T. rex specimen KUVP 5033 (“Bunker”), measures up to 1.63 m in length.
facts.quote: The largest known skull of Tylosaurus is T. rex KUVP 5033 (the "Bunker" specimen), estimated up to 1.63 m long

facts.statement: Tylosaurus skulls typically represent 13–14 % of the animal’s total body length.
facts.quote: skulls were between 13 and 14% of the total skeleton length

facts.statement: The head of Tylosaurus is strongly conical and its snout is proportionally longer than that of most mosasaurs, except Ectenosaurus.
facts.quote: The head was strongly conical and the snout proportionally longer than most mosasaurs, with the exception of Ectenosaurus

facts.statement: Tylosaurus is distinguished by an elongated, tooth‑less rostrum formed by the front ends of the premaxilla and dentary.
facts.quote: The most recognizable characteristic of Tylosaurus is the elongated edentulous rostrum that protrudes from its snout, for which the genus is named

facts.statement: The snout is reinforced by a broad, robust internarial bar composed of the posterodorsal process of the premaxilla, the nasals, and the anterior process of the frontal.
facts.quote: supported by a broad and robust internarial bar (comprising the posterodorsal process of the premaxilla, nasals, and anterior process of the frontal)

facts.statement: In Tylosaurus the prefrontal bones do not border the external nares because a long posterodorsal process of the maxilla excludes them.
facts.quote: unlike other mosasaurs, the prefrontal bones are excluded from the border of the nares by a long posterodorsal process of the maxilla

facts.statement: The nasal bones of Tylosaurus are either free‑floating or only lightly articulated to the internarial bar, never fused to each other, which makes them rare in the fossil record.
facts.quote: The nasal bones were either free-floating or lightly articulated to the internarial bar, did not contact the frontal, and were not fused to each other

facts.statement: The quadrate bone in adult Tylosaurus species is a robust, oval-shaped element that connects the lower jaw to the skull and supports the eardrum.
facts.quote: In adult forms for both species and in T. bernardi, T. pembinensis, and T. saskatchweanensis it takes on a robust oval-like shape.

facts.statement: The suprastapedial process of the quadrate likely served as the attachment point for muscles that opened the lower jaw.
facts.quote: it likely served as the attachment point for the depressor mandibulae muscles that opened the lower jaw.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus teeth are generally homodont, with marginal teeth of similar size and shape and smaller, more recurved pterygoid teeth.
facts.quote: The dentition is homodont, meaning that all teeth are nearly identical in size and shape, with the exception of the pterygoid teeth, which are smaller and more recurved than the marginal teeth.

facts.statement: In adult T. rex, the dentary bone makes up about 53‑57% of the total lower‑jaw length when combined with the overlapping splenial.
facts.quote: when combined with the overlapping splenial, about 53-57% in T. rex.

facts.statement: The marginal teeth of T. rex have finely serrated cutting edges (carinae) with small denticles.
facts.quote: Carinae (cutting edges) are finely serrated with small denticles in T. rex

facts.statement: Bardet et al. (2006) divided Tylosaurus species into a North American proriger group and a Euro‑American ivoensis group based on marginal tooth morphology.
facts.quote: Bardet et al. (2006) classified Tylosaurus species into two morphological groups based on marginal dentition.

facts.statement: The distinction of the ivoensis group is contentious among researchers.
facts.quote: The distinction of an ivoensis group is contentious.

facts.statement: Caldwell et al. (2008) argued that T. pembinensis cannot be compared with T. ivoensis because its teeth lack fluting.
facts.quote: Caldwell et al. (2008) argued that T. pembinensis cannot be compared with T. ivoensis as the former's teeth are not fluted

facts.statement: Adult Tylosaurus had unfused pectoral and pelvic girdles, unlike many other mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Both pectoral and pelvic girdles are unfused in adult Tylosaurus, in contrast to other taxa (e.g., Prognathodon overtoni).

facts.statement: Tylosaurus limbs retained primitive features, with humeri and femora lacking the complex muscle attachment sites seen in more derived mosasaurs.
facts.quote: Tylosaurus limbs are primitive relative to other mosasaurs; their stylopodia (humeri and femora) lack both the complex muscle attachment sites and extreme proximodistal shortening present in other derived taxa.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus displayed hyperphalangy, having more and spindle‑shaped phalanges than the ancestral condition.
facts.quote: Hyperphalangy (increased number of phalanges relative to the ancestral condition) is present in both fore- and hindlimbs, and the phalanges are spindle-shaped, unlike the short, blocky hourglass-shaped phalanges possessed by mosasaurines.

facts.statement: Scales of Tylosaurus were small, diamond‑shaped, keeled like shark denticles, and arranged in oblique rows similar to modern rattlesnakes.
facts.quote: These scales were small and diamond-shaped and were arranged in oblique rows, comparable to that found in modern rattlesnakes and other related reptiles.

facts.statement: A 5 m long Tylosaurus individual had dermal scales about 3.3 mm across, with roughly ninety scales per square inch on its underside.
facts.quote: An individual measuring 5 m in total body length had dermal scales measuring 3.3 x, and in each square inch (2.54 cm) of the mosasaur's underside an average of ninety scales were present.

facts.statement: Fossilized cartilage shows that Tylosaurus had a paired bronchi system suggesting two functional lungs, unlike snakes.
facts.quote: The pairing is suggestive of two functional lungs like modern limbed lizards but unlike snakes.

facts.statement: The bronchi bifurcation point in the examined Tylosaurus specimen lies between the first and sixth cervical vertebrae, a position similar to that of whales.
facts.quote: The bifurcation point for the Tylosaurus specimen is anywhere between the first and sixth cervical vertebrae.

facts.statement: The subfamily Tylosaurinae is defined by an elongated, tooth‑less premaxillary rostrum.
facts.quote: the subfamily is defined by a shared feature of an elongated premaxillary rostrum that does not bear teeth.

facts.statement: There is ongoing debate about whether T. kansasensis is a distinct species or a synonym of T. nepaeolicus.
facts.quote: there is still debate whether T. kansasensis is synonymous with T. nepaeolicus

facts.statement: The Tylosaurinae subfamily is estimated to have split from the Plioplatecarpinae about 93 million years ago, marking the fastest evolutionary rate among mosasaurid lineages.
facts.quote: The Tylosaurinae was approximated to have diverged from the Plioplatecarpinae around 93 million years ago; the divergence was characterized by the highest rate of evolution among all mosasaurid lineages.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus nepaeolicus is estimated to have diverged from the rest of its genus roughly 86.88 million years ago.
facts.quote: The Bayesian analysis also approximated a divergence of T. nepaeolicus from the rest of the genus around 86.88 million years ago

facts.statement: Tylosaurus proriger and Tylosaurus bernardi are estimated to have split from each other about 83.16 million years ago.
facts.quote: and a divergence between T. proriger and T. bernardi around 83.16 million years ago.

facts.statement: In the Western Interior Seaway, Tylosaurus nepaeolicus and T. proriger may represent a single, continuously evolving lineage (a chronospecies) that does not overlap stratigraphically.
facts.quote: In the Western Interior Seaway, two species—T. nepaeolicus and T. proriger—may represent a chronospecies, in which they make up a single lineage that continuously evolves without branching

facts.statement: Researchers have hypothesized that T. proriger evolved as a paedomorph of T. nepaeolicus, retaining juvenile skull features into adulthood.
facts.quote: proposed in 2016 that T. proriger evolved as a paedomorph of T. nepaeolicus, in which the descendant arose as a result of morphological changes through the retention of juvenile features of the ancestor in adulthood.

facts.statement: A later ontogenetic study found the paedomorphosis hypothesis unclear due to limited sample size of mature T. nepaeolicus specimens.
facts.quote: Zietlow (2020) found that it was unclear whether this observation was a result of paedomorphosis, although this uncertainty may have been due that the sample size of mature T. nepaeolicus was too low to determine statistical significance.

facts.statement: An alternative hypothesis suggests T. proriger evolved by peramorphosis, acquiring adult-like traits earlier in development.
facts.quote: the same study proposed an alternative hypothesis of peramorphosis, in which T. proriger evolved by developing traits found in mature T. nepaeolicus during immaturity.

facts.statement: The elongated, tooth‑less rostrum of Tylosaurus was originally proposed to function as a battering ram for stunning prey or deterring sharks.
facts.quote: Russell (1967) first speculated the elongated rostrum was used to "stun" prey or defend against sharks

facts.statement: In some Tylosaurus species, a double buttress secures the premaxilla‑maxilla suture, allowing the rostrum to lock under frontal impact.
facts.quote: the suture between the premaxilla and maxilla is also secured with a double buttress, which would allow the rostrum to lock in place upon a frontal force

facts.statement: Zietlow (2020) also found no evidence of sexual dimorphism related to rostrum growth in Tylosaurus.
facts.quote: Zietlow (2020) found no evidence of sexual dimorphism relating to rostrum growth.

facts.statement: The edentulous part of the Tylosaurus rostrum contains many foramina that transmit the ophthalmic nerve, indicating a dense sensory innervation.
facts.quote: the edentulous region of the rostrum contains numerous foramen that housed exits for the ophthalmic nerve, which transmits sensory information from the skin to the brain.

facts.statement: CT scans of a Taniwhasaurus skull revealed up to 16 branching terminals of the ophthalmic nerve within the rostrum, many exiting through external foramina.
facts.quote: they discovered a large network of internal canals of the ophthalmic nerve along the rostrum with up to 16 branching terminals inside the front end of the premaxilla, half of which exit into external foramina

facts.statement: The concentration of sensory nerves in the rostrum suggests it may have functioned as a mechanosensory or electrosensory organ, similar to adaptations seen in plesiosaurs and ichthyosaurs.
facts.quote: The high concentration of sensory nerves within the edentulous portion of the rostrum suggests that it housed a mechanosensory or electrosensory organ.

facts.statement: Gordon Bell noted that any injury to the Tylosaurus snout would have been extremely painful because of the dense nerve endings.
facts.quote: any injuries to the snout, such as if inflicted via ramming, would have been extremely painful due to the nerve endings.

facts.statement: The smallest known Tylosaurus neonate (specimen FHSM VP-14845) had a skull length of about 30 cm and a total length of roughly 2.23 m.
facts.quote: The youngest known Tylosaurus individual (FHSM VP-14845) is a newborn (neonate) estimated to have measured 30 cm in skull length and 2.23 m in total length

facts.statement: Mosasaurs, including Tylosaurus, are thought to have given birth to live young, although direct evidence for Tylosaurus has not yet been found.
facts.quote: Mosasaurs like Tylosaurus likely gave birth to live young. While no evidence has been attributed to Tylosaurus specifically, live birth has been documented in other mosasauroids

facts.statement: Skeletochronology of two juvenile Tylosaurus humeri indicated ages of 14 and 7 years at death.
facts.quote: The older humerus in Pellegrini's sample indicated the individual was 14 years old at death while the younger was aged 7 years

facts.statement: Both juvenile specimens showed rapid growth in the first few years, then a steadier rate after about year 5 in the older individual and year 6 in the younger, which may correspond to sexual maturity.
facts.quote: Both showed similar logarithmic growth curves that grew rapidly in the first few years but reduced to a steadier rate starting year 5 in the older specimen and year 6 in the younger. This may represent the ages when the individuals reached sexual maturity

facts.statement: The distance of first‑year growth rings in Tylosaurus humeri is greater than in Platecarpus and Clidastes, suggesting Tylosaurus was larger at birth.
facts.quote: The distance of first-year LAGs to the bone center in both specimens were longer than those in Platecarpus and Clidastes humeri, which suggests that Tylosaurus was larger at birth rather than being born at a similar size and then growing more rapidly

facts.statement: Zietlow concluded that some traits previously interpreted as growth stages actually represent interspecific variation, leading to the recognition of a new species, Tylosaurus rex.
facts.quote: suggesting that T. kansasensis was not an immature form of T. nepaeolicus, that their associated ontogram also contained a new species, and that her T. proriger ontogram was an amalgamation of T. proriger and another new species, which was later described as T. rex

facts.statement: Tylosaurus body temperature was considerably higher than that of coexisting cold‑blooded fish (Enchodus, 28.3 °C) and sea turtles (Toxochelys, 27.2 °C) and similar to the warm‑blooded seabird Ichthyornis (38.6 °C).
facts.quote: This was much higher than the body temperature of Enchodus and Toxochelys (28.3 C and 27.2 C respectively) and similar to that of Ichthyornis (38.6 C)

facts.statement: Because smaller mosasaurs like Platecarpus and Clidastes showed comparable body temperatures, Tylosaurus’s warmth is unlikely to be explained by gigantothermy.
facts.quote: The fact that the other mosasaurs were much smaller in size than Tylosaurus and yet maintained similar body temperatures made it unlikely that Tylosauruss body temperature was the result of another metabolic type like gigantothermy

facts.statement: Tylosaurus swam using carangiform locomotion, propelling itself mainly with its tail like mackerels.
facts.quote: it is now understood that Tylosaurus actually used carangiform locomotion, meaning that the upper body was less flexible and movement was largely concentrated at the tail like in mackerels.

facts.statement: Vertebral analysis of T. proriger shows rigid dorsal vertebrae but more flexible cervical, pygal and caudal vertebrae.
facts.quote: the dorsal vertebrae were relatively rigid but the cervical, pygal, and caudal vertebrae were more liberal in movement

facts.statement: Juvenile T. proriger specimens have stiffer cervical and dorsal vertebrae than adult individuals.
facts.quote: an examination of a juvenile T. proriger found that its cervical and dorsal vertebrae were much stiffer than those in adult specimens

facts.statement: Bite‑mark evidence indicates Tylosaurus also preyed on giant squid and ammonites.
facts.quote: Additional evidence from bite marks suggests the animal also preyed on giant squid and ammonites.

facts.statement: Puncture marks on ammonite shells, a Protostega carapace and an Enchoteuthis gladius have been attributed to Tylosaurus bites.
facts.quote: Puncture marks on fossils of ammonites, the carapace of a Protostega, and the gladius of an Enchoteuthis have been attributed to Tylosaurus.

facts.statement: The largest bite marks on the T. kansasensis specimen are about 4 cm long, matching the size of large mosasaur teeth.
facts.quote: The largest of the marks are about 4 cm in length, matching the size of large mosasaur teeth

facts.statement: Avascular necrosis was identified in every examined North American Tylosaurus skeleton and in the T. bernardi skeleton.
facts.quote: Examining 12 North American Tylosaurus skeletons and one T. bernardi skeleton, Rothschild and Martin (2005) identified evidence of avascular necrosis in every individual.

facts.statement: Between 3% and 15% of vertebrae in North American Tylosaurus and 16% of vertebrae in T. bernardi were affected by avascular necrosis.
facts.quote: The study observed that between 3-15% of vertebrae in the spinal column of North American Tylosaurus and 16% of vertebrae in T. bernardi were affected by avascular necrosis.

facts.statement: A juvenile Tylosaurus with a club tail had a shark tooth embedded in the fused vertebrae, indicating infection from a predator attack.
facts.quote: One juvenile specimen with the club tail condition was found with a shark tooth embedded in the fusion, which confirms that at least some cases were caused by infections inflicted by predator attacks.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus existed for roughly 20 million years and was endemic to the North Atlantic Circle Basin, including the Western Interior Seaway and Mediterranean Tethys above 30°N.
facts.quote: Throughout its ~20 million-year history, Tylosaurus was endemic to the North Atlantic Circle Basin, a geographic region comprising the North Atlantic and neighboring waters including the Western Interior Seaway in North America and Mediterranean Tethys in Europe above 30°N.

facts.statement: Russell (1967) suggested that Tylosaurus in the Niobrara Formation could have frequented open waters up to 400 km offshore.
facts.quote: Russell (1967) suggested that Tylosaurus in the Niobrara Formation frequented open waters far offshore, potentially up to 400 km from the nearest coastline in the WIS.

facts.statement: Kiernan (2002) found that Tylosaurus made up 57.7% of mosasaurs in shallow Santonian‑early Campanian deposits in Alabama but only 8.2% in offshore deposits of similar age.
facts.quote: Kiernan (2002) found that Tylosaurus comprised 57.7% of all mosasaurs found in Santonian to early Campanian deposits in Alabama that correspond to shallow continental shelves, and only 8.2% of mosasaurs in offshore deposits of similar ages.

facts.statement: Species assigned to Tylosaurus include T. proriger, T. nepaeolicus, T. pembinensis, T. rex, and T. saskatchewanensis.
facts.quote: subdivision: * T. proriger (Cope, 1869) (tipo) T. nepaeolicus T. pembinensis T. rex T. saskatchewanensis

facts.statement: The name Tylosaurus derives from the Greek words tylos meaning "protuberance" and sauros meaning "lizard".
facts.quote: Tylosaurus (del griego τυλος tylos "protuberancia" + σαυρος sauros "lagarto")

facts.statement: The name Tylosaurus was erected by Marsh in 1872 to include the original Harvard material and more complete specimens from Kansas.
facts.quote: Marsh finalmente erigió el nombre Tylosaurus recién en 1872, para incluir el material original de Harvard así como también los especímenes más completos que fueron hallados en Kansas.

facts.statement: A Tylosaurus specimen recovered in 1911 near Wallace, Kansas is one of the largest skeletons ever found and is displayed at the University of Kansas Natural History Museum.
facts.quote: Un espécimen de T. proriger, recuperado en 1911 por C. D. Bunker cerca de Wallace, Kansas es uno de los mayores esqueletos de Tylosaurus jamás hallados. Éste se encuentra actualmente en exhibición en el Museo de Historia Natural de la Universidad de Kansas.

facts.statement: In 1918 Charles H. Sternberg found a Tylosaurus with plesiosaur remains in its stomach, now mounted at the Smithsonian National Museum of Natural History.
facts.quote: En 1918, Charles H. Sternberg halló un Tylosaurus con restos de un plesiosaurio en su estómago. El espécimen se encuentra actualmente montado en el Museo Nacional de Estados Unidos (Smithsoniano) y los restos de plesiosaurio se conservan en las colecciones.

facts.statement: The stomach contents of that specimen were briefly reported in 1922 but were lost to science until rediscovered and described in 2004.
facts.quote: Aunque estos importantes especímenes fueron reportados brevemente por C. H. Sternberg (1922), la información se perdió para la ciencia hasta 2001. Este espécimen fue redescubierto y descrito por Everhart (2004a).

facts.statement: Specimens of Tylosaurus proriger reach lengths of 12.8 to 13.7 meters, making them among the largest mosasaurs.
facts.quote: los especímenes más grandes que se han encontrado contaban con longitudes de 12.8 a 13.7 metros.

facts.statement: Tylosaurus had an elongated, cylindrical premaxilla that may have been used to ram and stun prey or in intraspecific combat.
facts.quote: Una característica distintiva de Tylosaurus es su alargado y cilíndrico premaxilar (el hocico) del cual toma su nombre y el cual pudo haber usado para embestir y aturdir a sus presas y también pudo haberlo usado en combates intraespecíficos.

facts.statement: Stomach contents of Tylosaurus proriger show a varied diet of fish, sharks, smaller mosasaurs, plesiosaurs, and non‑flying marine birds such as Hesperornis.
facts.quote: Contenidos estomacales asociados con especímenes de Tylosaurus proriger indican que este feroz mosasaurio tenía una dieta variada, incluyendo peces, tiburones, mosasaurios menores, plesiosaurios y aves marinas no voladoras como Hesperornis.

facts.statement: Cone‑shaped bite marks on a hadrosaur skeleton from Alaska match the size and shape of Tylosaurus proriger teeth, suggesting scavenging by this mosasaur.
facts.quote: El tamaño, forma y espacio sin embargo, se parecen mucho a los dientes de Tylosaurus proriger.

facts.statement: A roughly 10‑meter Tylosaurus found in Kansas in 2009 is on display at the Museum of World Treasures in Wichita.
facts.quote: Un Tylosaurus de cerca de 10 metros de largo encontrado en Kansas por Alan Komrosky en 2009 está ahora en exhibición en el Museum of World Treasures en Wichita, Kansas.

facts.statement: The genus Tylosaurus lived from the Turonian to the Maastrichtian, about 93.9 to 66 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Turonian to Maastrichtian (93.9 to 66 million years ago)

facts.statement: Tylosaurus belongs to the subfamily Tylosaurinae within the family Mosasauridae.
facts.quote:
Parent group: Tylosaurinae
Family: Mosasauridae

rejected.statement: The species Tylosaurus rex was formally described as new by Zietlow and colleagues in 2026.
